messages.subject: Re: Expose Stan functions to R
parts:
I think we agree that if we can get by without (or with fewer regexps), then that would be good. But they work at the moment, so that is good enough for rstan. The next question is whether you can somehow make the entirety of the transformed parameters block, the model block, etc. into a function defined in the functions block so that you can then call it exactly in R?

Ben

On Wed, Mar 4, 2015 at 5:27 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
[is there a reason this isn't on stan-dev?]

Sebastian's e-mail seems to missing the juicy bits.

I would really rather not expose a pass-by-value vs. pass-by-reference
distinction in Stan --- it's one of the things users find really
confusing.

Regexes are not the long-term solution here --- we need to either

  1.  generate wrapper functions

  2.  code generate what's needed inside language/generator.hpp

Regexes are very very very brittle and will make it hard to put tests
into Stan to make sure we don't break them on the R side.

As a wise man (Jamie Zawinski apparently), once said,

  If you have a problem and think regexes are the solution,
  now you have two problems.

  http://blog.codinghorror.com/regular-expressions-now-you-have-two-problems/

- Bob

> I still think this would be hard, but perhaps as a first step in that direction, is it feasible to liberalize the syntax for functions so that they could take non-const references (perhaps with an explicit & in the Stan program) to arguments, as in
>
> void foo(matrix& x, matrix& y, matrix z) {
>   // modify x and y but not z
> }

> Then the user could implement their transformed parameters block as
>
> transformed parameters {

> I'm not sure within the Stan language how we could catch / prevent someone from passing a const thing like data or parameters to a non-const argument of a user-defined function, but then again I'm not sure how the parser currently catches / prevents a lot of things.
>
> Ben

> The next question is whether you can somehow make the entirety of the transformed parameters block, the model block, etc. into a function defined in the functions block so that you can then call it exactly in R?

Maybe. They'd have to run on an instantiated model though
with initialized parameters, because

On Thursday, March 5, 2015 at 2:05:13 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> But you pass the arguments to the user-defined functions back from the interface. So couldn't you just call your functions in the correct sequence? 

I'm afraid I don't understand what you mean.  What signature(s)
do you need from C++?

I guess it is possible to do the inputs automatically but I don't know how we could output multiple things without supporting tuples or doing pass by reference.
  • For a transformed data function, the inputs would be everything in data and the output would be everything in the transformed data block.
  • For a transformed parameters function, the inputs would be everything in data, transformed data, and parameters and the output would be everything in the transformed parameters block. 
  • For a model function, the inputs would be everything in data, transformed data, parameters, and transfomed parameters and void for output I guess.

Ben

> data and the output would be everything in the transformed data block.
> - For a transformed parameters function, the inputs would be everything

> in data, transformed data, and parameters and the output would be
> everything in the transformed parameters block.
> - For a model function, the inputs would be everything in data,

> transformed data, parameters, and transfomed parameters and void for output

This what I was thinking of when I suggested using JSON or Protocol
Buffers for input in this case as well. One could define a schema (and
serialization) for these inputs and then serialize them in R/Python,
passing them to Stan. They are small enough that we do not need to pass
by reference. We already have a "schema" for data and initialization
values (i.e., `var_context`) -- it's just currently treated as a special
case and has its own C++ class (but one could change this).

Yes, but also Sebastian and Aki have talked about using that for posterior predictive simulations, when they don't know everything that they want to simulate at build time.

I think I see. Are you imagining something like this:

void transformed_data(std::istream& data,
std::ostream& transformed_data);

So we'd read the data out of the input stream, run the data
transform, then write to the transformed data output stream.
All using JSON or protocol buffers?

And then for transformed data we could do this

void transformed_data(std::istream& data,
std::istream& parameters,
std::ostream& transformed_parameters);

Where it'd create the transformed data internally in this second call?
Or should it also have the transformed data as output? I wouldn't
want to allow transformed data as input to avoid inconsistencies.

That's definitely possible, but it'd take a while to refactor all
the code generation (which would probably be useful in and of itself).

- Bob
